title: Þ, Ð, Æ, Ǫ
subtitle: The four letters not found in modern English.
objectives: Pronounce þ and ð correctly in all positions.
Hear the difference between æ and ordinary a or e.
Pronounce ǫ as a distinct back rounded vowel.
Recognize these letters instantly in running text.

sections.heading: Þ and ð in detail
sections.body:
Þ (thorn) = voiceless th, as in thin, path, ether. Ð (eth) = voiced th, as in that, bathe, father. English has both sounds but writes them both 'th.' Old Norse distinguishes them in writing, though medieval scribes were inconsistent.

Where to use each: between vowels, usually ð (voiced). After voiceless consonants (s, t, p, k, f), usually þ (voiceless). Word-initial position varies by word: þú (you), ðat (that). Modern Icelandic has retained this distinction and can guide pronunciation, though the sagas predate sound changes in some consonant clusters.

sections.heading: Æ in detail
sections.body:
Æ (ash) is a low front vowel, the vowel in English cat or bad. It is always long in Old Norse. It developed from Proto-Germanic *ai by monophthongization. You will see it in common words: mæla (to speak), læra (to teach), hætta (to risk), and in names like Ægir (the sea-god).

Do not confuse it with the diphthong ei (which is two sounds: e + i) or with short e. Æ is one sound, held long.

sections.heading: Ǫ in detail
sections.body:
Ǫ (o-ogonek, sometimes printed ǫ or ö with a tail in older editions) is a back rounded vowel between o and a. Think of the vowel in English caught, law, oraw. It is distinct from both o and a. It developed from Proto-Germanic *a before certain consonants (especially before u in the next syllable, by u-umlaut).

Common words: sǫgn (tale), lǫnd (lands, plural of land), kǫttr (cat), ǫl (ale). It merged with ö in modern Icelandic, but in the saga age it was phonemically distinct.

letters.name: ash
letters.note: As in English cat. Always long.

letters.name: o-ogonek
letters.note: Back rounded vowel. As in caught.

sections.heading: Listening drill — minimal pairs
sections.instructions: Listen to pairs of words that differ only in one of these letters. Repeat each pair aloud.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Cover the answers and test yourself.

items.prompt: Which letter represents the voiceless th (as in thin)?
Which letter represents the voiced th (as in that)?

items.answer: No. It is a single vowel, always long.
Like the vowel in English caught or law. Back rounded, between o and a.
mahr (with voiced th in the middle, like the th in father)
thor (with voiceless th at the start, like thin)
mai-la (æ as in cat, held long)

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can pronounce all four special letters correctly in ten random words.
